STAGE 3 — EXERCISE GROUPS: diagnoses that share a problem share a programme
Each working diagnosis points (grey curved arrows) to one or two groups. A group = the shared mechanism + the exercises that target it + how to progress. Pick 3–5 exercises from the group, not all of them, and set the dose in Stage 4. Everyone finishes in the CORE PROGRAMME.
Why groups work: no single exercise type beats the others for chronic back pain (Hayden 2021; Owen 2020) — matching the direction of movement (Long 2004), the patient’s preference and a progressive dose matters more than the exact exercise.

LX-B · Early movement & mobility (“move it gently, don’t rest it”)
For: LD3 acute low back pain with mobility deficits (and any HIGH-irritability start)
SHARED PROBLEM: a sore, guarded, stiff back where fear and protective spasm limit movement; recovery is faster when people stay active.
• Walking: short bouts of 5–10 min several times a day, a little longer each day
• Cat–camel on hands and knees: 10 slow reps
• Knee rolls side to side lying on the back: 10 each way
• Pelvic tilts and gentle knees-to-chest: 10 reps
• Child’s pose / prayer stretch (sit back onto the heels): 3 × 20 s
• Heat wrap before moving if it helps (short-term relief, French 2006)
DOSE: little and often — every 2–3 hours; mild-to-moderate pain while moving is OK.
PROGRESS: within 1–2 weeks → LX-C or the core programme; return to work early on modified duties.
EVIDENCE: advice to stay active is recommended over bed rest (NICE NG59).

LX-A · Direction-specific repeated movements
For: LD1 extension preference · LD2 flexion preference · LD6 centralising sciatica · LD8 spinal stenosis
SHARED PROBLEM: pain that changes with one direction of movement; repeating the “good” direction calms it and restores movement.
EXTENSION BRANCH (LD1, LD6):
• Lying face down, relaxed, 2–3 min → propped on the elbows, 2–3 min
• Prone press-ups: 10 reps, hips stay down, straighten the arms as able
• Standing back-bends, hands on the hips: 10 reps (use at work or in the field)
• Sitting tall with a rolled towel behind the low back
FLEXION BRANCH (LD2, LD8):
• Knees-to-chest lying on the back: 10 reps or hold 20–30 s
• Pelvic tilts (flatten the back into the floor): 10 reps
• Seated forward bend between the knees: 10 reps
• Stationary cycling, or walking leaning on a stick or trolley
DOSE: 10 reps every 2–3 hours while symptoms are active.
RULE: keep going if leg symptoms move toward the back; STOP if they spread further down the leg.
PROGRESS: pain stays central → reintroduce the opposite direction gently → core programme.

LX-F · Bone-safe back-extensor strength & balance
For: LD12 stable osteoporotic vertebral fracture · older adults with a stooped (hyperkyphotic) back
SHARED PROBLEM: a weak, stooped back with fragile bones — the goals are extensor strength, upright posture and fewer falls.
• Lying face down (pillow under the tummy): lift the head and chest a little, 8–10 reps, hold 3 s
• Seated back extension against a chair back, shoulder blades squeezed: 10 reps
• Wall stand — heels, buttocks, shoulders and head toward the wall: 5 × 10 s
• Sit-to-stand and mini squats with a hip-hinge (no rounding); heel raises
• Balance: tandem stance and heel-to-toe walking beside a support
• Daily walking
AVOID: sit-ups, toe touches, twisting with load, lifting from the floor with a rounded back.
EVIDENCE: back-extensor exercise → 2.7 times fewer vertebral fractures at 10 years (Sinaki 2002); exercise guidance from Too Fit To Fracture (Giangregorio 2014).

LX-D · Nerve-friendly movement (calm the nerve, then load it)
For: LD7 non-centralising sciatica · LD6 centralising sciatica (once the leg pain has centralised)
SHARED PROBLEM: a sensitive, irritated nerve root that dislikes being stretched or squeezed but improves with gentle movement and blood flow.
• Positions of ease: lying with the calves on a chair; side-lying with a pillow between the knees
• Seated nerve slider: sitting tall, straighten the knee while looking up, then bend the knee while looking down — 10–15 smooth reps, no stretch pain
• Lying slider: hold behind the thigh; straighten and bend the knee while pointing and pulling up the foot — 10 reps
• Short walks several times a day
• Then rebuild the muscles of that nerve root: bridges, sit-to-stand, step-ups, heel raises
DOSE: sliders 10–15 reps, 2–3 times a day; any symptoms must settle within minutes.
RULE: numbness or pain spreading further down = too much — stop and step down.
AVOID: holding long hamstring or “sciatic” stretches.
EVIDENCE: neural mobilisation reduced pain (about 1.8 points out of 10) and disability in chronic low back pain (Basson 2017).

LX-C · Motor control & trunk–hip strength
For: LD4 movement-control impairment (incl. stable slip, healed pars fracture) · LD9 sacroiliac joint pain · LD10 pregnancy-related pelvic girdle pain
SHARED PROBLEM: the trunk and pelvis don’t control load well — catching, giving way, or pain when weight passes through the pelvis.
• Bracing — gently tighten the tummy and pelvic floor, keep breathing: 10 × 10 s
• Bird-dog on hands and knees, opposite arm and leg: 6–10 each side, hold 5–10 s
• Side-bridge from the knees → from the feet: 3–5 × 10 s each side
• Curl-up, hands under the low back, head and shoulders only: 5–10 × 10 s
• Bridges: 10–15 reps → single-leg bridges
• Hip-hinge with a stick along the spine → lift a light load from chair height
PELVIC GIRDLE BRANCH (LD9, LD10): side-lying leg lifts, clams, standing hip extension, single-leg stance holding a support, step-ups; pelvic belt short-term; in pregnancy use side-lying and hands-and-knees versions instead of lying flat.
DOSE: holds 6–10 × 10 s once or twice daily → 2–3 sets of 8–12 under load.
EVIDENCE: motor control / stabilisation is among the most effective exercise types for chronic back pain (Owen 2020); the Hicks 2005 rule picks likely responders.

LX-E · Graded activity, aerobic conditioning & pain education
For: LD5 chronic non-specific back pain · LD11 widespread pain / central sensitisation · LD8 stenosis (walking programme) · anyone with a HIGH STarT Back score
SHARED PROBLEM: a sensitised, deconditioned system and fear of movement — the aim is confidence and capacity, not finding “the right muscle”.
• Pain education: hurt ≠ harm; flare-ups are expected and settle
• Walking programme: start at 70–80% of today’s comfortable time or distance; add about 10% a week (by plan, not by pain)
• Graded exposure: list feared activities (bending, lifting, floor sitting) and practise them in small, safe steps
• Whole-body strength: sit-to-stand, wall push-ups, rows with a band or water bottles, step-ups
• Yoga- or Pilates-style classes, tai chi, cycling, swimming — whatever they enjoy
• Relaxed breathing and a regular sleep routine
DOSE: build toward 150 minutes of moderate activity a week plus 2 strength days (WHO 2020 physical activity guidelines).
RULE: progress by the plan (time-contingent), not by how the pain feels that day.
EVIDENCE: exercise reduces pain in chronic back pain with no clear best type (Hayden 2021); stratified, psychologically informed care improved disability and saved costs (Hill 2011).

LX-CORE · CORE PROGRAMME FOR EVERYONE — where every group ends up
Once symptoms are settling, every patient moves here. For chronic back pain the evidence favours any well-dosed, enjoyable, progressive programme over the “perfect” exercise.
STRENGTH (2–3 days a week, 2–3 sets of 8–12): sit-to-stand → squat holding a water pot; hip-hinge → lifting a sack or bag from a step; split squats or step-ups; rows with a band; carrying practice (two equal loads, then one-sided).
ENDURANCE: walking, cycling or swimming, building to 150 minutes a week.
WORK AND LIFE TASKS: practise the patient’s own PSFS goals — floor sitting and rising, squatting toilet, lifting a child, carrying water, field-work postures, riding a two-wheeler.
FLARE-UP PLAN: drop back one level for 2–3 days, keep walking, use the group’s easing movement, then rebuild.
WHY KEEP GOING: 69% of people have another episode within 12 months of recovering (da Silva 2019); exercise with education cut the risk of a new episode by about 45% (Steffens 2016).
